final.title: Eval drift is a threshold decision, not a theory problem
final.body:
If you automate a recurring workflow, eval drift is not an abstract AI issue. It is the question of how you will notice the system no longer fits the work it was built for.

For a small business, that often shows up in customer replies, invoices, or lead handling. A workflow that looked fine on a sample set can start slipping once real messages, edge cases, or a process change enter the picture. The useful move is to define the workflow, the measurable outcome, and the stop rule before you automate.

Here is the practical part: pick one observable threshold and one human review point. For example, you might decide that if more than a small share of items is being flagged for manual review, the workflow needs to pause and be checked. That is an illustration, not a Bareni measurement.

For money movement and other high-risk decisions, human approval stays mandatory. The machine can alert you that patterns have changed; it should not quietly keep going as if nothing happened. That would be optimistic, which is not the same as controlled.

A good next step is to write one sentence for the workflow: “If X changes, we pause automation and review Y.” That turns eval drift into an operational boundary you can actually run.

final.title: Designing against eval drift starts with a threshold
final.body:
If you are automating a recurring workflow, eval drift is not a theory problem. It is the question of how you will know the system is no longer matching the work it was built to handle. In a small business, that often shows up in customer replies, invoices, or lead handling. The AI may look fine on the sample you used to build it, then real messages, edge cases, or a process change start pulling it off course.

The practical move is to define the workflow, the measurable outcome, and the stop rule before you automate. For example, if an assistant is classifying inbox messages, decide what “correct enough” means and what level of manual review means the system needs a reset. That threshold is a control, not a promise.

For owner-operators, the boundary stays human. If the workflow touches money movement or any other high-risk decision, the machine should not decide on its own. Build for alerts, review, and a clear handoff back to you when confidence drops or patterns change. That is design intent, not a claim that the system already does it.

The next step is simple: write one sentence for the workflow, such as, “If X changes, we pause automation and review Y.” Then ask two questions: how would I know it is drifting, and what decision do I want to keep?】【。
